Question: In a small pond there are eleven lily pads in a row labeled \(0\) through \(10.\) A frog is sitting on pad \(1.\) When the frog is on pad \(N,\) \(0 \lt N \lt 10,\) it will jump to pad \(N - 1\) with probability \(\dfrac{N}{10}\) and to pad \(N + 1\) with probability \(1 - \dfrac{N}{10}.\) Each jump is independent of the previous jumps. If the frog reaches pad \(0\) it will be eaten by a patiently waiting snake. If the frog reaches pad \(10\) it will exit the pond, never to return. What is the probability that the frog will escape being eaten by the snake?
Solution:
The frog's current pad contains all the information needed for its future jumps. Let \(p_i\) be the probability of reaching pad \(10\) before pad \(0\), starting from pad \(i\). The endpoint values are \(p_0=0\) and \(p_{10}=1\). Conditioning on the first jump gives, for \(1\le i\le9\),
\[
p_i=\frac{i}{10}p_{i-1}+\frac{10-i}{10}p_{i+1}.
\]
This equation involves three neighboring probabilities. Taking differences turns it into a recurrence involving just two neighboring differences. Define
\[
d_i=p_i-p_{i-1}\qquad(1\le i\le10).
\]
Rearranging the first-step equation gives
\[
(10-i)d_{i+1}=i d_i,
\]
so
\[
d_{i+1}=\frac{i}{10-i}d_i\qquad(1\le i\le9).
\]
Every denominator here is positive. Starting with \(d_1\), the first five differences are \(d_1\) times
\[
1,\quad\frac19,\quad\frac1{36},\quad\frac1{84},\quad\frac1{126}.
\]
For example, \(d_3=(2/8)d_2=d_1/36\). Continuing the recurrence gives the same five multipliers in reverse order for \(d_6,\ldots,d_{10}\).

Adding all the differences cancels the intermediate probabilities, leaving
\[
\begin{aligned}
1=p_{10}-p_0&=\sum_{i=1}^{10}d_i\\
&=2d_1\left(1+\frac19+\frac1{36}+\frac1{84}+\frac1{126}\right)\\
&=\frac{146}{63}d_1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore \(p_1=d_1=63/146\).

It remains to check that the frog cannot avoid both endpoints forever with positive probability. From any interior pad, consecutive left jumps reach pad \(0\) in at most nine jumps. Each such jump has conditional probability at least \(1/10\), so this path has probability at least \(10^{-9}\). Consequently, for every positive integer \(r\), the probability of avoiding both endpoints for \(9r\) jumps is at most
\[
(1-10^{-9})^r,
\]
which approaches zero. Thus the frog eventually reaches an endpoint with probability \(1\), and its probability of escaping the snake is \(\boxed{\frac{63}{146}}\), choice C.
